# READ ME
## Generated by: Sam Slane  
## For: RPI Independent Project - uArch Modeling
## Project: Microarchitectural Modeling and OS Interface of an IOPS-Optimized Domain-Specific Core  


### Project Statement
This project proposes to investigate, model, and quantify the potential of a IOPS core microarchitecture on the host's side. The core research question is: how can the co-design of a lightweight host microengine and a minimalistic interface maximize the effective IOPS and reduce tail latency for AI IO patterns, when interfacing with ultra low latency next-gen SSDs? The focus will be on microarchitectural modeling (creating an optimized simulated engine to perform IO processing), data collection (recording the time spent in block layer during actual Windows reads/writes), and performance quantification (comparing the two and displaying differences via tables and graphs). This project's deliverables are a simulation model (with a top layer in (```testbench.sv```)), an analytical report (```report.md```), a literature review of relavent papers (```Notes/literature_review.md```), and a visualization of the compared data between hardware and software (```Figures/*```). Althought the visualizations for this project are much less helpful than the explination given in the report. <br>
IMPORTANT!!! An important thing to note about this project is that it has existed in two versions. Version 1 of the project was made for the Advance Computer Harwader class at RPI in Fall 2025. While the project did process commands and output statistics, it was not an accurate respresentation of the Windows I/O stack. Version 2 of the project, which is made for an Independent Project class at RPI in Spring 2026, is a much more accurate representation of the Windows I/O stack. Files that end with "-DEPRICATED" are from verion 1 of the project, and do not apply to the current code.

### Solution Description
The solution created is a hardware simulation created in SystemVerilog. My idea was to take the current block layer (including the queue and NVMe drivers) in the Windows IO stack and to copy it into hardware. This way the process could be parallelized, and also just be faster in general due to the lack of software/kernel/OS overhead. Implemented in SystemVerilog is essentially the entire Window's I/O stack, including an IRP manager; a block layer processor; the real NVMe drivers with proper queue managing, admin control, and doorbell registers; a msi interrupt controler, an IO processor, a PCIe bridge, and finally performance gathering modules and a testbench. The code was modeled to be as accurate as possible to their Window's software equivalents in the kernel. There are two key changes that exist between this code and the real hardware stack. Change one is that the NVMe queues were made in series instead of parallel. This removes the performance improvement (and actually is a massive performance slow down), but is easier to implement. A lot of effort was put into trying to get the parallel queues' of NVMe to work and sadly none were successful. Change two is that the completion queue is not completely implemented. The code that models the completion queue in the program right now simply mimics the inputs and outputs of a command queue, but it does not implement an actual queue. Doorbells are still rung, head and tail pointes are updated, and data is read, but there is no formal queue built into the program. Both of these changes were purely due to a lack of time in tinkering with the code and getting everything to work. With more time, it is possible and reasonable to implement these missing features.

Summary: The innovation of this project is in accurately translate the Windows IO stack from software to hardware, removing software overhead.

### Running the Project

**To generate a new hardware_output.txt:**  
In line 419 of testbench.sv, change the path to where you have this project stored. Also change the path on line 520. 
I recommend running 70_cpu_commands.txt as the code was tested on 70 commands and 7 commands may show unusual or unexpected behavior.

Simulate involved_hardware_blockqueue.sv in ModelSim. Do not run it using iverilog (Icarus Verilog), as it does not have the ability to run this file.

**DEPRICATED: To generate a new software_output.txt:**  
Change the SSD latency to your SSD's latency in analysis.py (lines 24 and 25)  
Change the CPU frequency to your CPU's frequency in analysis.py (line 66)  

Optional: Run run_io_trace.bat and use Windows Performance Recorder to generate a new .etl file for your computer.  
Optional: Then find the average disk service time in Windows Performance Analyzer and calculate block layer overhead from that number.  
Optional: Replace BLOCK_LAYER_OVERHEAD_PER_CMD in analysis.py (line 20) with the new calculated value (in ns)  

Run software_build.bat in CMD (```software_build.bat```)
Run block_layer_test.exe in CMD (```block_layer_test.exe```)

This entire block is depricated because the hardware output is no longer compared to a software equivilent.

**DEPRICATED: To generate new figures:**  
Once software_output.txt and hardware_output.txt have been generated, run analysis.py in cmd (```python analysis.py```).
The figures are depricated for the same reason that generated software results is depricated.
The code will run and make new graphs (if the file paths are fixed), but they all show essentially the same data, which is that the new project is worse in every metric compared to the old parallelized project.
